research.domain: Energy system: the largest cause of climate change, and the transition away from fossil fuels

sources.name: Ember – Yearly Electricity Data (global + Europe), with the Global Electricity Review 2026
sources.measures: Annual electricity generation by source (TWh), share of generation (%), installed capacity (GW), lifecycle emissions (MtCO2e), emissions intensity (gCO2e/kWh), demand and net imports (TWh), and year-on-year changes. Sources: Solar, Wind, Hydro, Bioenergy, Other renewables, Nuclear, Coal, Gas, Other fossil, plus aggregates (Clean, Fossil, Renewables, Wind and solar).
sources.coverage: Annual, 2000–2025. 215 countries and areas plus aggregates (World, continents, EU, OECD, G20, G7, ASEAN). A separate US dataset covers all 50 states.
sources.latest_release: Global Electricity Review 2026 (first full 2025 data) came out 21 Apr 2026. The landing page says 'Last Updated: 15/09/2026'. The global CSV I fetched had last-modified 22 Sep 2026.
sources.update_cadence: Rolling updates twice a month (first and third weeks), with a major annual release in April (Global Electricity Review).
sources.format: CSV, one row per area × year × source with metrics as columns (about 16 MB). Long-format legacy CSV (about 49 MB). JSON through API v1, which needs a free API key tied to an email.
sources.license: CC BY 4.0. The page footer says content is under the Creative Commons Attribution Licence (CC-BY-4.0), and the API OpenAPI spec declares the same licence. Note from the methodology: renewable capacity comes from IRENA and fossil capacity from GEM, so those values have upstream terms (see the IRENA and GEM entries).
sources.citation: Ember does not publish a fixed citation string. Recommended form (matches OWID usage): "Ember (2026). Yearly Electricity Data [dataset], accessed YYYY-MM-DD. https://ember-energy.org/data/yearly-electricity-data/. Licensed under CC BY 4.0." For the report: "Ember (2026), Global Electricity Review 2026, 21 April 2026."
sources.status: Active. Non-profit and philanthropically funded, so not exposed to US federal cuts. Bulk files are updated continuously.
sources.url_check: WebFetch of the landing page gave the CSV URLs, 'Last Updated: 15/09/2026', and the CC-BY-4.0 footer. curl -I on release_generation_yearly_global.csv returned HTTP 200, 16,084,305 bytes, last-modified Tue 22 Sep 2026. The header row starts 'Area,ISO 3 code,Year,Area type,Electricity source,Is aggregated source,Generation (TWh),...'. Parsed World 2025: Solar 2,780.204 TWh (8.737%), Wind 2,704.379 TWh, Coal 10,610.915 TWh (33.347%), Clean 42.309%, Fossil 18,357.373 TWh, Total 31,820.135 TWh, intensity 460.503 gCO2e/kWh. The long-format CSV returned 200 (49 MB, generation timestamp 23 Jun 2026). api.ember-energy.org returned '{"detail":"No API key set"}' without a key, and its openapi.json gives licence CC-BY-4.0, version 1.2.0. The GER 2026 page gave a 21 April 2026 publication date.
sources.site_use: Backbone of the electricity layer: global and country electricity mix (stacked area), clean versus fossil share, solar overtaking wind and coal, carbon intensity of each country's grid (used for the 'is an EV or heat pump cleaner where I live' calculator), and country rankings. Store each ingested CSV snapshot with its SHA-256 and last-modified date so every number shown carries a vintage.
sources.caveats: (1) Emissions are lifecycle CO2e from UNECE factors, not combustion CO2. Never add them to Global Carbon Project numbers. (2) Values get revised between vintages. The April GER reported renewables at 33.8% of 2025 generation and coal at 33.0%; the September CSV shows 33.48% and 33.35%. Pin the vintage. (3) The most recent year is partly estimated for some countries. (4) EU yearly data are gross generation, monthly data are net. (5) Demand = generation + net imports.

sources.name: Ember – Monthly Electricity Data
sources.measures: Monthly generation by source (TWh), share (%), lifecycle emissions (MtCO2e), emissions intensity (gCO2e/kWh), demand, and year-on-year changes.
sources.coverage: Monthly. 88 geographies covering more than 90% of global power demand (99 area labels including aggregates in the CSV). Dates run 1998-12 to 2026-08 depending on country. The World aggregate runs 2019-01 to 2026-07.
sources.latest_release: The page says 'Last Updated 28 July 2026', but the CSV I fetched had last-modified 18 Sep 2026 and data through Jul 2026 for World and Aug 2026 for some countries.
sources.format: CSV (about 28 MB). Also available through API v1 (key required).
sources.license: CC BY 4.0 (stated on the page footer).
sources.citation: "Ember (2026). Monthly Electricity Data [dataset], accessed YYYY-MM-DD. https://ember-energy.org/data/monthly-electricity-data/. CC BY 4.0."
sources.url_check: WebFetch of the landing page gave the CSV URLs, the 88-geography coverage, and CC BY 4.0. curl -I returned HTTP 200, 28,333,064 bytes, last-modified Fri 18 Sep 2026. Parsed World for 2026-07-01: Solar 331.495 TWh, 11.277% share, +15.157% YoY. Fossil 1,660.813 TWh, YoY -0.886% (-14.838 TWh). Clean 43.503%.
sources.site_use: A 'pulse of the transition' strip on the home page showing the latest month's solar and clean share and fossil generation YoY. Also seasonal small multiples by country. Label it clearly as monthly and provisional.
sources.caveats: Provisional and revised often. The World monthly total is Ember's estimate built from covered countries, so it is not a sum of all 215 countries. Same lifecycle-emissions caveat as the yearly data.

sources.name: Energy Institute – Statistical Review of World Energy 2026 (75th edition)
sources.publisher: Energy Institute (with KPMG and Kearney; Ember is the electricity partner; S&P Global Commodity Insights is a knowledge partner)
sources.measures: Total energy supply / primary energy by fuel (EJ), oil, gas and coal production, consumption, trade, reserves and prices, electricity generation by fuel, renewables, energy-related CO2 (Mt), and critical minerals.
sources.coverage: Annual, mostly 1965–2025. About 80+ countries reported individually, plus regions.
sources.latest_release: 2026 edition, published 30 Jun 2026. OWID snapshot metadata gives date_published 2026-06-30. Press coverage confirms the 75th edition with 2025 data.
sources.format: XLSX ('EI-Stats-Review-ALL-data.xlsx', about 4 MB), a narrow-format consolidated CSV (about 21 MB), a panel-format file, and a PDF.
sources.license: © Energy Institute 2026. Terms are at https://www.energyinst.org/terms, which I could not fetch (HTTP 403, Cloudflare). EI's published guidance, which I saw only via search snippets: quoting with attribution to the Statistical Review is welcome, but extensive reproduction of tables or charts needs EI's prior permission. Redistributing data sourced from S&P Global is prohibited without S&P authorisation. This is not an open licence.
sources.citation: "Energy Institute – Statistical Review of World Energy (2026)." This is the OWID-documented form and matches EI attribution guidance. Long form: "Energy Institute (2026), Statistical Review of World Energy 2026, 75th edition, London."
sources.status: Active, but every page and file is behind a Cloudflare bot challenge. OWID's own 2026 ingestion script says the files must now be downloaded by hand.
sources.url_check: curl and WebFetch of /statistical-review/resources-and-data-downloads returned HTTP 403 with a Cloudflare 'Just a moment...' challenge. The PDF under /__data/assets/ also returned 403. I did not bypass the challenge. Indirect checks: the OWID etl snapshot snapshots/energy_institute/2026-06-30/*.dvc lists both files with license '© Energy Institute 2026' and md5 values, and its .py docstring confirms the Cloudflare challenge and manual download.
sources.site_use: The authoritative total-energy picture (fossil share of TES, energy mix by fuel). Display it through the OWID energy dataset with EI attribution. Before offering bulk CSV downloads of EI-derived columns, ask EI for written permission at statisticalreview@energyinst.org (address from search snippet, not verified). For any chart whose CSV must be fully redistributable, use EIA International (public domain) or Ember (CC BY) as that chart's single canonical source instead. Do not mix sources inside one series.
sources.caveats: Licence ambiguity for bulk redistribution. EI headline growth rates are leap-year adjusted: EI says TES rose 1.7% in 2025, while the raw TWh ratio in OWID gives +1.37% because 2024 had 366 days. Document this or activists will find an apparent mismatch. EI moved to 'total energy supply' accounting, which differs from the older substitution method.

sources.name: Our World in Data – Energy dataset (new TES-methodology release; legacy owid/energy-data)
sources.publisher: Our World in Data (Global Change Data Lab)
sources.measures: 130 columns per country and year: total energy supply by source (TWh, %, per capita, annual change), electricity mix (TWh, %, per capita), electricity demand, net imports, lifecycle emissions and carbon intensity, fossil fuel production, population, and GDP.
sources.coverage: 1700/1800–2025 (World back to 1800 via Smil). Countries plus OWID-defined regions and source-defined regions (e.g. 'Europe (EI)'). 19,494 rows × 130 columns.
sources.latest_release: New dataset CSV last-modified 30 Sep 2026. It uses EI 2026 (published 2026-06-30) and Ember yearly data accessed 2026-04-24. The legacy GitHub dataset is frozen; the README transition banner was committed 2026-10-01.
sources.update_cadence: Irregular, following each upstream release (EI in July, Ember several times a year).
sources.format: CSV (about 9 MB), XLSX, codebook CSV, sources CSV, Markdown readme. The Grapher API gives a CSV plus metadata JSON per chart.
sources.license: OWID: all visualisations, data and code produced by Our World in Data are open access under CC BY. Third-party data stays under its original terms. EI-derived columns carry '© Energy Institute 2026' (OWID origin metadata). Ember columns are CC BY 4.0. EIA columns are public domain. OWID's indicator metadata has a 'nonRedistributable' flag; it is False for the EI indicators.
sources.citation: "Energy Institute – Statistical Review of World Energy (2026) and other sources – with major processing by Our World in Data." This is the readme's 'How to cite this data'. Per-indicator citations are in owid_energy.sources.csv.
sources.status: Active, but in transition. The legacy files (owid-public.owid.io) are 'no longer updated'. OWID says it is 'working on a better home for this dataset', so the URL may move again.
sources.url_check: Read the GitHub README via raw.githubusercontent.com: it has the transition banner, legacy changelog (last entry 2026-04-27), and the CC BY statement. The GitHub API commits list shows the latest commit 2026-10-01. Fetched the readme.md, sources.csv and codebook.csv. Streamed owid_energy.csv (HTTP 200, 9,081,888 bytes, last-modified 30 Sep 2026) and parsed World 2025: total_energy_twh 166,753.6 (= 600.3 EJ), fossil_fuels_energy_share_pct 86.238434, low_carbon_energy_share_pct 13.761562, solar_electricity_twh 2,778.64. The metadata JSON for indicator 1295381 shows EI origin license '© Energy Institute 2026' and nonRedistributable False.
sources.site_use: The single cleanest machine-readable source for the total-energy layer (fossil share of energy, energy per capita, energy mix by country) and long-run history (1800–). In the ingestion pipeline, make the metadata 'nonRedistributable' flag a hard gate: fail the build if it is true. Do not silently substitute another source.
sources.caveats: (1) Methodology changed in 2026: energy is now total energy supply, not the substitution method, so figures are not comparable with older OWID charts activists may have saved. (2) The Ember vintage lags Ember's own site: 2025 solar is 2,778.64 TWh here versus 2,780.204 TWh in Ember's September CSV. (3) OWID region aggregates differ from EI and Ember regions. (4) OWID growth rates are not leap-year adjusted, unlike EI's. (5) Pre-1965 world values come from Smil (2017).

sources.name: U.S. EIA Open Data API v2 and bulk files (electricity, SEDS, International)
sources.publisher: U.S. Energy Information Administration (U.S. Department of Energy)
sources.measures: US electricity generation, consumption and capacity by state, sector and fuel (Forms EIA-923 and EIA-860), prices, US energy-related CO2, and the International dataset (production and consumption by country and fuel, quad Btu and TWh, plus CO2).
sources.coverage: US monthly and annual, state level (electricity from 2001). International annual 1980–2024 for about 220 countries.
sources.latest_release: API v2 (v2.1.11, Jan 2026). Annual US generation for 2025 is already in the API. INTL.zip last-modified 3 Oct 2026, with World primary energy for 2024.
sources.update_cadence: Monthly (Electric Power Monthly); International updated several times a year.
sources.format: JSON REST API (5,000-row page limit, free API key) and zipped bulk JSON-lines files.
sources.license: Public domain. The EIA reuse page says US government publications are in the public domain and not subject to copyright. EIA requests an acknowledgement in the form 'Source: U.S. Energy Information Administration (<Month Year>)'.
sources.citation: "Source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Electric Power Operational Data (Form EIA-923), API v2, accessed YYYY-MM-DD." For international data: "U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) – International Energy Data (2026)."
sources.status: At risk. Reporting in 2025 (Reuters, Argus, ProPublica, Energy Intelligence) described the loss of about 100+ staff (around 40% of the workforce), delayed reports (International Energy Outlook, US Energy-Related CO2 Emissions, uranium reports), and the discontinued Annual Solar PV Module Shipments report. The API and core monthly electricity data were working on 2026-10-04. Archive every pull.
sources.url_check: Fetched the copyrights_reuse page and quoted its public-domain terms. GET https://api.eia.gov/v2/?api_key=DEMO_KEY returned a route list (coal, electricity, international, ...). The electricity query returned 2025 US totals: ALL 4,429,501.6 thousand MWh, COW (coal) 737,150.7, SUN 295,671.4, WND 464,390.6, and 2024 ALL 4,308,634.3, COW 652,155.9. The international query returned World primary energy consumption of 606.04 quad Btu for 2024. api.eia.gov/bulk/INTL.zip redirects 301 to www.eia.gov/opendata/bulk/INTL.zip, which returned 200 (24,153,479 bytes, last-modified Sat 03 Oct 2026).
sources.site_use: US drill-down: US → state → fuel → (later) plant. A public-domain international primary-energy series is useful wherever a chart's CSV must be fully redistributable. US coal generation rising in 2025 (+13%) is a strong teaching point.
sources.caveats: Primary energy methodology differs from EI (quad Btu, different conversion of non-fossil electricity), so never mix EIA and EI in one series. International data lag EI by about one year. The API key belongs in macOS Keychain or CI secrets, never in the repo. Federal capacity risk is real.

sources.name: IRENA – Renewable Capacity Statistics 2026 and IRENASTAT (PxWeb API)
sources.measures: Installed electrical capacity (MW) and electricity generation (GWh) by technology (solar, wind, renewable hydro, bioenergy, geothermal, marine, pumped storage, fossil fuels, non-renewable totals), by country or region and grid connection. Also renewable share of capacity and generation. Finance table: public investments (2023 million USD).
sources.coverage: Annual 2000–2025 for capacity. World and 9 regions, plus about 200 countries and areas.
sources.latest_release: Publication released 31 Mar 2026 (ISBN 978-92-9260-725-8). IRENASTAT tables 'ELECSTAT_2026_H2' were updated 2026-09-28T17:56–18:11.
sources.update_cadence: Capacity statistics are published annually in March, with a fuller Renewable Energy Statistics edition in July. IRENASTAT tables are refreshed every half-year, and their table IDs change with each version (e.g. *_2026_H2_PX.px).
sources.format: PxWeb JSON API: GET returns metadata, POST a JSON query to get CSV or JSON. Also trilingual PDF tables.
sources.license: Publication terms: material may be freely used, shared, copied, reproduced, printed and stored, provided it is clearly attributed to IRENA and carries a copyright notation (© IRENA) with the year. Third-party material may have separate terms, including restrictions on commercial use. Separately, the IRENASTAT web footer says '© IRENA ... All Rights Reserved'.
sources.citation: "IRENA (2026), Renewable capacity statistics 2026, International Renewable Energy Agency, Abu Dhabi." For the API pull: "IRENA (2026), IRENASTAT Online Data Query Tool, table Region_ELECSTAT_2026_H2, accessed YYYY-MM-DD. © IRENA 2026."
sources.url_check: irena.org HTML pages returned 403 to WebFetch and curl, but the PDFs under /-/media/ returned 200. Extracted the full PDF p.2 and got the ISBN, the citation, and the free-use and © notation terms. The highlights PDF says 5,149 GW at end-2025, +692 GW, 49.4% renewables share of total capacity, and a 2024 revision from 4,443 to 4,457 GW. The PxWeb API root returned the table list with 'updated' timestamps. A POST to Region_ELECSTAT_2026_H2 for World capacity returned Total Renewable 2024 = 4,461,631.67 MW, 2025 = 5,155,007.33 MW; Solar 2025 = 2,396,709.19 MW; Wind 2025 = 1,291,015.04 MW; Fossil fuels 2025 = 4,629,715.61 MW.
sources.site_use: Charts of capacity growth (solar and wind installed GW by country), renewables' share of new capacity, and an 'additions per year' bar chart. Pair with Ember generation to show the difference between capacity and generation.
sources.caveats: Numbers are revised between vintages (5,149 GW in March versus 5,155 GW in the September API), so always show the table version. Capacity is not generation: solar's capacity factor is much lower than nuclear's. Table IDs change every half-year, so the pipeline should discover them from the API listing and fail loudly if a table is missing. Licence wording differs between the publications and the web tool; consider asking IRENA for written confirmation.

sources.name: IRENA – Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2025 (report and data file)
sources.measures: Global and country levelised cost of electricity (LCOE, USD/kWh in constant 2025 USD), total installed costs (USD/kW), capacity factors, and auction prices for solar PV, onshore and offshore wind, CSP, hydro, geothermal and bioenergy. New in this edition: firm LCOE of solar-plus-storage hybrids and battery installed costs.
sources.coverage: 2010–2025 global weighted averages, with longer history for some technologies. Country series for major markets.
sources.latest_release: Published July 2026 (OWID datePublished 2026-07-01; data file last-modified 2 Jul 2026; ISBN 978-92-9260-749-4).
sources.format: XLSX (12.9 MB) with one sheet per report figure ('Fig 1.1', 'Fig 2.3', ...), not tidy. PDF.
sources.license: Unless otherwise stated, material may be freely used, shared, copied, reproduced, printed and stored, provided IRENA is acknowledged as the source and copyright holder. Third-party material may need separate permission. OWID records the licence as '©IRENA 2026'.
sources.citation: "IRENA (2026), Renewable power generation costs in 2025, International Renewable Energy Agency, Abu Dhabi."
sources.url_check: curl -I on the XLSX returned 200 (12,908,268 bytes, last-modified Thu 02 Jul 2026). openpyxl listed sheets 'Contents', 'Fig S.1', 'Fig 1.1', ... 'Fig 3.1'. Extracted exec summary PDF pp.2–4: citation, terms, and the highlights 'Solar PV remained at its 2024 level of USD 44 per MWh', onshore wind USD 33/MWh, offshore USD 78/MWh, solar down 89% since 2010, >90% of new utility-scale capacity cheaper than the cheapest new fossil option, and 8.4 Gt CO2 avoided. OWID levelized-cost-of-energy CSV, World: solar_photovoltaic 2010 = 0.40771458, 2025 = 0.043538958 USD2025/kWh.
sources.site_use: The 'why the transition is now economic' chart: LCOE by technology from 2010 to 2025, with fossil-fuel cost bands as context. Feeds the 'what you can do' story (solar plus storage is cheapest in most markets).
sources.caveats: Global weighted averages hide large country differences (China solar USD 36/MWh versus far higher elsewhere). LCOE excludes system integration costs. OWID combines the 2025, 2024 and 2023 reports and deflates older values with the US GDP deflator; values from 2010 onward come from the 2025 report. The XLSX layout changes every year, so the parser must be written per vintage and validated against the PDF.

sources.name: Our World in Data – learning-curve series: solar PV module prices and lithium-ion battery cell prices
sources.publisher: Our World in Data, compiling Nemet (2009), Farmer & Lafond (2016) and IRENA for solar, and Rupert Way (2026, in preparation) for batteries
sources.measures: Solar PV module price (constant 2025 US$/W) against cumulative installed capacity (MW). Li-ion battery cell price (constant 2024 US$/kWh).
sources.coverage: Solar modules 1975–2024 (cumulative capacity to 2025). Battery cells 1991–2024. World only.
sources.latest_release: Solar series lastUpdated 2026-07-28. Battery series lastUpdated 2025-11-19 (origin dated 2026-01-08).
sources.license: Solar: the Nemet component is CC BY 3.0 (Santa Fe Performance Curve Database), and the 2010+ component is ©IRENA with free-use terms. Battery: OWID lists the licence as CC BY 4.0, but the dataset was 'shared with Our World in Data via private communication' and includes BloombergNEF and Avicenne inputs. nonRedistributable is False for both indicators.
sources.citation: Solar: "IRENA (2025); Nemet (2009); Farmer and Lafond (2016) – with major processing by Our World in Data." Battery: "Rupert Way (2026) based on Ziegler and Trancik (2021), BloombergNEF, and Avicenne Energy – with minor processing by Our World in Data."
sources.status: Active (OWID). The battery series' upstream is not publicly archived.
sources.url_check: Fetched both metadata JSONs and the origins listed above. Battery CSV, World: 1991 = 9,210.23, 2022 = 132, 2023 = 111, 2024 = 78 (constant 2024 US$/kWh). Harvard Dataverse API for doi:10.7910/DVN/9FEJ7C: license None, terms say the dataset was made available without information on how it can be used, and both .tab files are restricted. Solar metadata processing notes: 1975–2003 from Nemet, 2004–2009 from Farmer & Lafond, 2010+ from IRENA pvXchange, deflated with the US GDP deflator.
sources.site_use: Learning-curve hero chart: 'every doubling of solar deployment cut module prices by roughly X%', on a log-log scale. The battery cell price decline appears on the EV drill-down with a visible provenance warning.
sources.caveats: Activists cannot trace the battery series past OWID: the BNEF component is proprietary, the Ziegler & Trancik files are restricted, and the compilation came by private communication. Flag it 'secondary – upstream not public'. The solar series stitches three sources with different methods (module price indices).

sources.name: IEA – Global EV Outlook 2026 and Global EV Data Explorer
sources.measures: EV sales, stock, sales share and stock share (cars, buses, vans, trucks, 2/3-wheelers; BEV and PHEV), charging points, EV oil displacement (mb/d), battery deployment (GWh), and electricity demand. Projections to 2035 (STEPS/APS) exist but should not be shown as data.
sources.coverage: Historical 2010–2025. Roughly 40+ countries plus regions and World.
sources.latest_release: GEVO 2026, typeset May 2026. PDF last-modified 19 Jun 2026. Data explorer last updated 20 May 2026 per IEA listings (seen via search; iea.org itself returned 403).
sources.format: PDF. Undocumented CSV API at api.iea.org/evs: the parameters filter seems to be ignored and all parameters are returned. XLSX on the data-product page probably needs a free IEA account (not verified).
sources.license: The PDF's licence page says the work is under CC BY 4.0, subject to the IEA's Notice for CC-licensed Content, and every page footer reads 'IEA. CC BY 4.0.' The IEA CC notice says OECD/IEA does not necessarily own every component, and third-party components are used at the user's risk. GEVO draws on third parties (EV Volumes, Marklines, ACEA and others).
sources.citation: "IEA (2026), Global EV Outlook 2026, IEA, Paris https://www.iea.org/reports/global-ev-outlook-2026, Licence: CC BY 4.0" (as recorded in OWID origin metadata).
sources.status: Active. iea.org blocks automated fetchers (HTTP 403); the blob storage and api.iea.org are reachable.
sources.url_check: curl -I on the blob PDF returned 200 (20,175,354 bytes). Parsed with pypdf: 295 pages, licence text on p.294, and the exec summary on p.10 says electric car sales grew 20% to exceed 20 million in 2025, one-quarter of new cars. api.iea.org/evs without a region returned 400 'Must specify a region or a year'; with region=World it returned CSV rows such as 'World,Historical,EV sales share,Cars,EV,2025,percent,25', 'EV sales ... 21000000', 'EV stock ... 75000000', 'EV stock share ... 5', 'Oil displacement, Mbd ... 1.2'. The iea.org product pages returned 403.
sources.site_use: Transport drill-down: EV sales share by country (Norway, China, EU, US), stock, and oil displaced. Combine with the Ember or EIA grid intensity for each country to show the lifecycle advantage of an EV on that grid.
sources.caveats: API values are rounded (21,000,000; 75,000,000), so use the XLSX for exact values once account access is confirmed. 'EV' includes plug-in hybrids. The API is undocumented and could change; snapshot every pull. The battery chapter gives a pack-price index, not absolute $/kWh. Do not use other IEA datasets on the assumption they are CC BY; many are not (see the World Energy Balances entry).

sources.name: IEA – World Energy Investment 2026 (report and datafile)
sources.measures: Global and regional energy investment (USD, real), split into clean energy (renewables, nuclear, grids, storage, low-emissions fuels, efficiency, electrification) and fossil fuel supply and power.
sources.coverage: About 2015–2026 (2026 is an estimate). World and major regions.
sources.latest_release: Launched 28 May 2026 (launch presentation dated 'Paris, 28 May 2026'). PDF last-modified 19 Jun 2026. Datafile 'last updated June 2026' per IEA listing (seen via search only).
sources.format: PDF. XLSX datafile on the IEA product page (not fetched: 403, probably needs a free account).
sources.license: Search snippets of the IEA product page describe the datafile as a free product under CC BY 4.0. I could not verify this directly (iea.org returned 403), and the PDF licence page did not extract. Treat it as CC BY 4.0, pending confirmation.
sources.citation: "IEA (2026), World Energy Investment 2026, IEA, Paris https://www.iea.org/reports/world-energy-investment-2026, Licence: CC BY 4.0"
sources.url_check: curl -I on the blob PDF returned 200 (17,403,451 bytes, last-modified 19 Jun 2026). pypdf (260 pages), p.6: total investment USD 3.4 trillion in 2026, up 5% from 2025, with about USD 2.2 trillion to clean energy and about USD 1.2 trillion to oil, gas and coal. The datafile product page returned 403.
sources.site_use: A 'follow the money' panel: clean versus fossil investment over time, set beside fossil fuel subsidies (IMF, OECD).
sources.caveats: 2026 figures are estimates, not outturn. The 'clean' definition is broad (grids, efficiency, nuclear). Licence and exact datafile values must be verified by a logged-in human download before publishing CSVs.

sources.name: Global Energy Monitor – Global Coal Plant Tracker (and sibling trackers)

sources.coverage: 14,674 units in 111 countries (per the page): operating units, proposals since 2010, and retirements since 2000.
sources.latest_release: July 2026 release. The summary sheet says the data is based on the Global Coal Plant Tracker, updated July 2026. Annual analysis: Boom and Bust Coal 2026 (May 2026).
sources.format: Summary tables as Google Sheets (CSV export works). Full unit-level XLSX through a download web form, which is JavaScript-rendered; I could not verify which fields it asks for.
sources.license: CC BY 4.0. GEM states that its tracker data are freely available under the CC BY 4.0 International Public License unless otherwise noted (seen via search). GEM's licence page (fetched) contains the standard CC BY 4.0 legal text. Exception in a sibling tracker: Global Solar Power Tracker records sourced from TransitionZero are CC BY-NC 4.0.
sources.citation: "Global Coal Plant Tracker, Global Energy Monitor, July 2026 release." (exact wording on the tracker page)
sources.url_check: WebFetch of the tracker page gave 'July 2026' and the citation. Parsed the page HTML and mapped 28 summary-table Google Sheet links to their titles. CSV export of 'Coal Plants by Country (MW)' returned the header 'Country/Area,Announced,Pre-permit,Permitted,Announced + Pre-permit + Permitted,Construction,Shelved,Cancelled (since 2010),Operating,Mothballed,Retired (since 2000)' and TOTAL row '298,225 | 98,935 | 105,584 | 502,744 | 260,301 | 105,665 | 1,817,068 | 2,226,469 | 45,028 | 536,549' MW. The download-data page HTML contains a form titled 'Download the Global Coal Plant Tracker dataset'.
sources.site_use: Map and country drill-down of the coal fleet: what operates, what is being built, what is planned to retire, and who owns it. Use the 'Planned Coal Plant Retirements' and ownership tables for local action pages (e.g. 'coal plants near you and their retirement dates'). Sibling trackers (oil and gas extraction, solar, wind) can be added the same way.
sources.caveats: Capacity is not generation: coal capacity grew 3.5% in 2025 while coal generation fell (Boom and Bust Coal 2026). Unit-level data needs the form download and a human step, with a snapshot hash kept. Google Sheets URLs can change between releases. Check the licence of each sibling tracker (CC BY-NC in solar).

sources.license: The hub licence field is 'custom', pointing to IMF Copyright and Usage (https://www.imf.org/external/terms.htm, which returned an empty page or 403). Per search snippets of IMF's special terms for IMF Data: reuse, derivatives and redistribution are allowed if data appear accurately and are attributed, e.g. 'Source: International Monetary Fund'. Data owned by third parties is excluded.

IMF Working Paper WP/25/270, International Monetary Fund, Washington DC. The hub records cite instead: Black, Liu, Parry and Vernon (2023), IMF Fossil Fuel Subsidies Data: 2023 Update, ISBN 9798400249006.
sources.status: Active, but the hub lags the latest update. imf.org and elibrary.imf.org returned 403 to automated fetch.
sources.url_check: The hub v3 API returned name 'Fossil Fuel Subsidies', modified 1777467927554 (= 2026-04-29), recordCount 7056, licence custom → IMF terms. A FeatureServer query returned fields Country, ISO3, Indicator (e.g. 'Explicit Fossil Fuel Subsidies - Coal'), Unit ('Percent of GDP' or 'USD at constant 2021 prices') and F2015…F2030. Headline 2024 figures come from the 2025 WP, while country-level machine-readable data on the hub is still the 2023 Update (constant 2021 USD); do not mix vintages. A human must download the 2025 data file from imf.org (not verified).

drilldown_paths: WHERE OUR ENERGY COMES FROM (cause): World total energy supply by fuel, 1800–2025 (OWID energy / EI 2026) → pick a country → per-capita energy compared with the world average → split into electricity and other energy uses (Ember demand as a share of TES) → for electricity, the country's mix by source (Ember yearly) → each fuel's trend. Series: owid_energy.csv (total_energy_twh, *_energy_share_pct, *_energy_per_capita_kwh), Ember release_generation_yearly_global.csv.

FROM FUEL TO CO2 (cause → consequence link): fossil CO2 by fuel, World 1750–2024 (GCB 2025v15) → country (territorial and per capita) → that country's coal power fleet (GEM: operating, under construction, retirement year, owner) → its grid carbon intensity in gCO2e/kWh (Ember, labelled lifecycle) → hand-off to the emissions and impacts domains (concentration, temperature). Series: GCB2025v15_MtCO2_flat.csv, GEM summary sheets, Ember emissions intensity.

HOW FAST IS THE TRANSITION? Clean share of world electricity, yearly 2000–2025 and monthly to July 2026 (Ember) → solar and wind generation by country (Ember) → installed capacity and annual additions (IRENASTAT) → why it is happening: LCOE by technology 2010–2025 (IRENA RPGC 2025) and the solar module learning curve 1975–2024 (OWID/Nemet/IRENA) → where the money goes, clean versus fossil investment (IEA WEI 2026). Series: Ember yearly and monthly, IRENA Region/Country_ELECSTAT_2026_H2, IRENA RPGC data file, OWID solar-pv-prices-vs-cumulative-capacity, WEI 2026.

TRANSPORT AND YOU: EV share of new car sales by country, 2010–2025 (IEA GEVO API) → EV stock and oil displaced (mb/d) → battery cell price decline (OWID/Way, shown with an 'upstream not public' badge) → 'Is an EV cleaner on my grid?', which takes the user's country or US state and multiplies grid gCO2e/kWh (Ember, or EIA for US states) by a transparent, cited kWh/km. Series: api.iea.org/evs, Ember emissions intensity, EIA electric-power-operational-data.

UNITED STATES TO STATE TO FUEL: US generation by fuel, 2001–2025 (EIA API v2, public domain), including coal's 2025 rebound (652 → 737 TWh) → pick a state → its fuel mix and trend → its coal plants and planned retirements (GEM US sheets) → local action (utility resource plans, community solar). Series: EIA electricity/electric-power-operational-data (location=state), Ember US electricity data, GEM 'Coal Plants in the United States (MW)'.

FOLLOW THE MONEY (policy levers): clean versus fossil investment, 2015–2026e (IEA WEI) → fossil subsidies by country, explicit versus implicit and by fuel (IMF, vintage-labelled) → named support measures in a country (OECD Inventory SDMX, e.g. Germany's electricity price compensation) → what reform achieves (IMF estimates: explicit-subsidy removal cuts CO2 about 6% by 2035 and avoids about 70,000 premature deaths a year). Series: WEI 2026, IMF FeatureServer or 2025 file, OECD DSD_FFS@DF_FFS_<ISO3>.

WHO IS LEFT OUT (consequence and justice): people without electricity (655 million in 2024) and without clean cooking (about 2 billion), by country (WDI / Tracking SDG7) → set against per-capita energy use (OWID) and per-capita fossil CO2 (GCB) → shows that high emitters and low-access countries are different places. Series: WDI EG.ELC.ACCS.ZS and EG.CFT.ACCS.ZS, owid_energy per-capita columns, GCB per-capita CSV.

THE PULSE (live view): the latest month's world solar share, clean share and fossil YoY (Ember monthly) → country small multiples → link to the yearly context. Series: release_generation_monthly_global.csv.
research.action_links:
INDIVIDUALS: (1) Electrify what you can, and let the grid data decide the impact. Ember (yearly, lifecycle gCO2e/kWh by country) and EIA (by US state) show how clean electricity is where the visitor lives. That turns 'switch to an EV or heat pump' into a locally sourced calculation rather than a generic claim. IEA GEVO 2026 shows EVs already displaced about 1.2 mb/d of oil in 2025 (api.iea.org/evs, 'Oil displacement, Mbd' 2025 = 1.2). (2) Rooftop or community solar, and choosing clean tariffs: IRENA RPGC 2025 finds that more than 90% of new utility-scale renewables commissioned in 2025 were cheaper than the cheapest new fossil option, and solar PV LCOE is about USD 44/MWh. The site must give no personal financial advice; it presents cost data only.
COMMUNITIES AND ACTIVISTS: (3) Coal plant retirements. GEM's 'Planned Coal Plant Retirements (MW)' and ownership sheets (CC BY 4.0, July 2026) name the plants, owners and retirement dates. Combined with EIA (US) or Ember country data, an activist can cite exactly which plant, how many MW, and its estimated annual CO2 (GEM 'Coal Plants by Country: Annual CO2'). (4) Utility resource plans and public comment: use EIA state fuel mix plus IRENA costs to argue that new gas or coal costs more than renewables plus storage (IRENA firm LCOE for solar plus battery is below USD 85/MWh at high-quality sites in 2025).
POLICYMAKERS: (5) Subsidy reform. IMF WP/25/270 estimates that removing explicit fossil subsidies ($725 bn in 2024) would cut CO2 about 6% by 2035, avoid about 70,000 premature air-pollution deaths a year, and raise revenue of about 0.6% of GDP. It also finds the poorest 20% receive only about 8 cents per subsidy dollar (RePEc abstract). The OECD Inventory names the specific measures (SDMX DSD_FFS). (6) Investment direction: IEA WEI 2026 shows clean energy at about USD 2.2 tn versus fossil at USD 1.2 tn in 2026, so the remaining gap is a policy choice. (7) Energy access: Tracking SDG7 2026 reports 655 million people without electricity, mostly in Sub-Saharan Africa. Every action page should link to the exact series and vintage behind each claim, with the same citation strings given in the sources list.
research.gaps_and_risks:
LICENCE RISKS: (a) The Energy Institute Statistical Review is the canonical total-energy source, but it is '© Energy Institute'. Its guidance requires permission for extensive reproduction of tables or charts and prohibits redistributing S&P Global-sourced data, and its files sit behind a Cloudflare challenge (HTTP 403; OWID now downloads them by hand). Before publishing bulk CSVs of EI-derived numbers, get written permission from EI. Otherwise, pick a fully open canonical source per chart: Ember (CC BY) for electricity, EIA International (public domain) for total energy. Never blend sources within one series. (b) IEA: only some products are CC BY 4.0 (GEVO 2026 confirmed in the PDF; the WEI 2026 datafile is CC BY per IEA listings but not directly verified). World Energy Balances and most IEA data are Non-CC and must not be redistributed. iea.org blocks automated fetching, product XLSX files probably need a free account (a human step), and the EV API is undocumented with rounded values. CC BY does not clear third-party components (EV Volumes and others). (c) Battery prices: there is no fully open, traceable absolute $/kWh series. BNEF is paywalled, Benchmark is flagged nonRedistributable by OWID, the Ziegler & Trancik Dataverse files are restricted, and the OWID/Way compilation came 'via private communication'. Show it with a provenance badge or use IEA's index. (d) IRENA: publications allow free use with attribution and a © IRENA notation, but the IRENASTAT web footer says 'All Rights Reserved', and third-party material may restrict commercial use. Get written confirmation. (e) The GEM Solar Power Tracker has CC BY-NC records (TransitionZero), and GEM full datasets go through a download form.
VINTAGE AND REVISION RISKS: Ember revised the 2025 renewables share from 33.8% (April GER) to 33.48% (September CSV) and coal from 33.0% to 33.35%. The 'renewables overtook coal' headline holds only narrowly, so pin vintages. IRENA moved from 5,149 to 5,155 GW. The OWID energy dataset changed methodology to total energy supply (October 2026) and its Ember vintage lags Ember's own site. EI growth rates are leap-year adjusted (TES +1.7% versus a raw +1.37%). The IMF Climate Data hub still serves the 2023 Update while headlines come from the 2025 Update. Mitigation: immutable snapshot of every ingested file (URL, fetch time, HTTP last-modified, SHA-256, and producer version string), with that provenance attached to every number and every downloadable CSV. That fits the under-$20/month budget: all files are under 50 MB and can be fetched on a schedule into object storage.
METHOD MISMATCHES TO DOCUMENT, NEVER MIX: Ember lifecycle CO2e versus GCB combustion CO2 versus EI energy CO2. Substitution versus TES versus EIA quad-Btu primary energy. IMF price-gap/externality subsidies versus OECD budget-based support. Capacity (GW) versus generation (TWh). Projections (IEA STEPS, WEI 2026 estimates) are not observations.
STATUS AND AVAILABILITY RISKS: US EIA lost about 40% of staff in 2025, with reports delayed or discontinued (e.g. Annual Solar PV Module Shipments), so archive EIA pulls. NREL appears to have been renamed (IRENA acknowledgements list 'NLR'), and the NREL Annual Technology Baseline was not assessed and may be at risk. Hosts that block automated fetchers (IEA, IMF, OECD, IRENA HTML, EI) mean some ingests need a documented manual step. GEM summary tables live in Google Sheets whose IDs can change between releases.
COVERAGE GAPS NOT FILLED HERE: final energy use by sector (buildings, industry, transport) without IEA balances (EIA SEDS covers only the US). Methane from oil, gas and coal supply (IEA Methane Tracker is CC BY 4.0 per IEA's CC list; belongs to the emissions or methane domain). Fossil fuel production plans versus 1.5°C (UNEP Production Gap Report; GEM oil and gas extraction tracker) not assessed. Heat pump sales (IEA, licence unverified). Grid and storage deployment (IRENA has pumped hydro; battery storage capacity open data is thin). Clean-energy jobs (IRENA annual review not assessed). Lazard LCOE+ was not used (proprietary).
UNVERIFIED ITEMS TO CONFIRM BEFORE LAUNCH: the exact text of EI's terms page; the WEI 2026 datafile licence and XLSX URL; the GEVO 2026 XLSX URL and login requirement; the IMF 2025 country data file URL and DOI; the OECD FFS DOI and the missing USA dataflow; the fields on the GEM download form; the Tracking SDG7 2026 report licence (the report may differ from WDI's CC BY 4.0); the EI permission contact address.
